name: The Narrator
summary: An unnamed wanderer whose consuming instinct for 'the strange and the unknown' leads him alone into the nameless city, where he uncovers an underground gallery of mummified reptilian beings and barely survives an eruption of their still-living kin from the abyss beneath the ruins. The same name is also attached, in a separate account, to a shell-shocked sailor who resolves to end his own life after glimpsing a monstrous sea-creature and its idol.
description:
The unnamed narrator is a recurring first-person voice in Lovecraft's fiction, appearing here as a solitary antiquarian who deliberately defies the warnings of nearby Arabs and journeys alone by camel into a parched, terrible valley to explore the nameless city, an urge he attributes to 'that instinct for the strange and the unknown which had made me a wanderer upon earth and a haunter of far, ancient, and forbidden places.' Digging among the obliterated edifices with tools he had brought, he clears a buried aperture and, torch in hand, descends through a natural cavern and an artificial rock-hewn passage into a subterranean gallery lined with glass-fronted cases holding the mummified remains of a reptilian race, and reads their painted history as an allegorical epic of the city's rise and fall.

Pressing toward a brazen gate at the corridor's end, he beholds a luminous abyss beyond and collapses from exhaustion and dread, aware that among all the reptile relics his is the only human form — save for one figure shown torn to pieces in the final fresco. A rising moan and a gathering gale from the depths herald the return of the city's ancient inhabitants: amid a howling wind he babbles the couplet of 'the mad Arab Alhazred, who dreamed of the nameless city,' and glimpses a nightmare horde of devil-like reptiles surge past him back into the earth, the great brazen door clanging shut behind them.

He is left saying that some unnamed power 'guided him back to life,' though he expects forever to 'shiver in the night wind till oblivion — or worse' claims him. A separate account under the same name — that of a shell-shocked survivor of a Pacific sea-disaster — instead resolves to leap from a garret window rather than face a similar horror, a discrepancy that may indicate two distinct unnamed narrators sharing a generic name.
fate: He resolves to end his own life after writing his account, believing an immense slippery creature is at his door and that 'the end is near.'

sources.quote: I am writing this under an appreciable mental strain, since by tonight I shall be no more.
The end is near. I hear a noise at the door, as of some immense slippery body lumbering against it. It shall not find me. God, that hand! The window! The window!
I alone have seen it, and that is why no other face bears such hideous lines of fear as mine
I was quite unbalanced with that instinct for the strange and the unknown which had made me a wanderer upon earth and a haunter of far, ancient, and forbidden places.
what Abaddon guided me back to life, where I must always remember and shiver in the night wind till oblivion—or worse—claims me

facts: He was traveling in a parched and terrible valley under the moon when he first saw the nameless city.
He alone has seen the nameless city, and no other face bears such hideous lines of fear as his.
No other man shivers so horribly as he does when the night wind rattles the windows.
He defied the Arabs' warnings and went into the untrodden waste with his camel.
He had many tools and dug much within the walls of the obliterated edifices.
He cleared a sand-choked aperture with his spade and crawled through it, carrying a torch, to enter a temple.
He saw the moon gleaming over the ruins and a cloud of sand blown by a wind from a temple ahead.
He traced the wind to the black orifice of a temple and entered it after the wind died down.
He found the temple larger than others he had visited, presumably a natural cavern, with low altars and curvilinear carvings.
He discovered a small artificial door chiselled in solid rock leading to a steeply descending passage of tiny steps.
He descended the narrow passage for what felt like an immense distance until his torch died out.
In the darkness he recalled fragments of demoniac lore and recited verse to keep from despairing.
He reached a level floor and crept through a dark passage lined with wood-and-glass cases resembling coffins.
He saw a glow ahead and discovered a richly painted underground hall containing mummified reptilian creatures in the cases.
He theorized the reptile creatures were sacred to the city's people, comparable to the she-wolf of Rome or an Indian tribe's totem-beast.
He imagined an epic history of the nameless city based on the frescoes he saw, including its rise, decline, and final descent into the earth.
He described himself as having an instinct for the strange and the unknown that made him a wanderer and haunter of forbidden places.
He crept along the underground corridor toward brighter light while studying the frescoes.
He recognized the passages depicted in the painted epic as ones he himself had traversed.
He crept up to a gate at the end of the hall and cried aloud in amazement at the void of light beyond.
He looked at the steps leading into the abyss but did not dare try them, touched the open brass door and could not move it, then sank prone to the stone floor from exhaustion.
He felt a throb of fear on realizing his was the only human form among the reptile relics, save the man torn apart in the last painting.
He was suddenly seized by acute fear and gazed back along the corridor toward the tunnels leading to the outer world.
He heard a deep, low moaning sound and felt an increasing draft of cold air flowing from the tunnels and the city above.
He checked his watch and saw sunrise was near, then braced himself against the gale sweeping down into the cavern.
He dropped prone and clutched at the floor for fear of being swept into the abyss.
He compared himself to the man who was torn to pieces by the nameless race.
He believed he screamed frantically and was almost mad.
He tried to crawl against the wind but was pushed slowly toward the unknown world.
His reason snapped and he babbled the couplet of the mad Arab Alhazred.
He saw a nightmare horde of devil-like reptile creatures outlined against the abyss.
He was plunged into darkness after the great brazen door clanged shut behind the creatures.
He survived the ordeal, guided back to life by unknown means, but remains haunted, expecting to shiver in the night wind till oblivion or worse claims him.
